To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
neonatal glucocorticoid treatment at high dosage results in a precocious micro- and macromorphologic lung development with a second round of alveolarization.

neonatal high-dose short-term glucocorticoids applied to the rat lung result in precocious alveolarization with a subsequent step back in the alveolar process followed by an almost complete recovery of the lung parenchyma.

short-term high-dosage glucocorticoid treatment in the neonatal rat lung leads to a marked acceleration of the lung maturation process, with an early microvascular septation and a subsequent alveolarization, followed by a step back in maturational state and an exceptional second round in the alveolar maturation process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of neonatal high-dose short-term glucocorticoids on lung development in the rat.
the effects of glucocorticoids on lung maturation and development in a rat model.
the question of whether the application of glucocorticoids in the neonatal period has any long-lasting effects on the lung.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

glucocorticoids can be safely applied in the neonatal period for the treatment of respiratory distress syndrome and chronic lung disease, but only when the dosage and duration of treatment are carefully adjusted.

glucocorticoids can induce an accelerated maturation process in the rat lung, which is, however, followed by a step back and a second round of the maturation process, resulting in a normal lung phenotype.
glucocorticoid administration during the first 4 d of postnatal life in rats results in a precocious maturation of the lung with a subsequent recovery to the normal phenotype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a short-term, high-dosage treatment with glucocorticoids during the first postnatal weeks results in an accelerated lung maturation with an almost complete recovery of lung structure by the time the animal reaches adulthood.
a short-term application of high-dosage glucocorticoids to the rat lung results in a precocious maturation of microvascular septa and an acceleration of alveolarization.
a short-term, high-dose glucocorticoid treatment in the neonatal period is not necessarily associated with long-term adverse side effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a short-term high-dosage glucocorticoid treatment can have long-term effects on the lung, which can only be revealed by long-term follow-up of the treated animals.
the lung is a very dynamic organ, which is able to recover even from severe insults.
a careful and short-term application of glucocorticoids can be a useful tool for the treatment of respiratory distress in neonates, with minimal long-term effects on lung development.
